22:9.text: For the LORD our God, he it is that brought us up and our fathers out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage, and which did those great signs in our sight, and preserved us in all the way wherein we went, and among all the people through whom we passed:

provenance.other: “our fathers out of the land” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Joshua 24:17. The wider formula “brought thee out of the land of” occurs in four (Exodus 20:2, Deuteronomy 5:6, Deuteronomy 13:10, Psalm 81:10), and in every one of them the land is Egypt. The Book of Mormon substitutes Jerusalem, which is the one substitution the phrase cannot make in the KJV.
provenance.significance: The king is not asking a neutral question. He identifies God by the only formula the King James Bible has for identifying him — the deliverance of the fathers out of a land — and Joshua 24:17 is the verse where that formula is a people's answer at a covenant renewal, the reply to 'choose you this day whom ye will serve' and to Joshua's charge to put away 'the gods which your fathers served on the other side of the flood'. A Lamanite king who has just granted the Amalekites their sanctuaries is given the words of Israel renouncing its inherited gods, twelve verses before he does exactly that. The exchanged land is the point as well: Egypt is the house of bondage the fathers left, and for this book the land the fathers left is Jerusalem, so the creed arrives intact with one word moved.

22:9.note: 'Is God that Great Spirit that brought our fathers out of the land of Jerusalem?' The five-word run 'our fathers out of the land' is a KJV singleton, and the sentence around it is the standard KJV confession of God by his exodus — the preface to the Decalogue at Exodus 20:2, the people's creed at Joshua 24:17 — with Jerusalem where the KJV always has Egypt. Joshua 24 is preferred over Exodus 20 for the run itself ('our fathers', not 'thee') and for the setting: Joshua 24 is a confession made by a people choosing between the LORD and the gods of their fathers, which is the choice in front of this king. Note that the king reaches this creed unprompted; Aaron has said nothing about an exodus. The formula is presented as something the Lamanites already have, which is the chapter's premise about them.

22:12.text: So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.

provenance.other: The preposition is again not Genesis 1:27's. “created man in his own image” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 1:27; “after his image” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 5:3, of Adam begetting Seth. The 1830 reads 'after his own image', which is in no KJV verse at all — it is 1:27's possessive fitted to 5:3's preposition, the same fusion recorded at Alma 18:34 (where Colossians 3:10 supplies the parallel). 'Transgression' is likewise not Genesis's word for the fall; “Adam's transgression” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 5:14.
provenance.significance: What Aaron is described as doing is not quoting Genesis but reading it, and the summary tells us which Genesis he read: creation in the image, a commandment given, a transgression, a fall. That is the sequence of Genesis 1-3 as Romans 5 abstracts it, not as Genesis narrates it — Genesis 3 has a serpent, a woman, a tree and a curse, and Aaron's precis has none of them. The catalogue's interest is that a scene about a man reading scripture to a king reproduces the chapter divisions of a Pauline summary rather than the events of the text being read.
provenance.alternative: Genesis 9:6, 'for in the image of God made he man', the KJV's other statement of the doctrine.

22:12.note: 'He began from the creation of Adam, reading the Scriptures unto the king; how God created man after his own image, and that God gave him commandments, and that because of transgression, man had fallen.' Hardy's apparatus cross-references Genesis 1:26-3 here, and the verse is a compressed recital of exactly that span: image (1:26-27), commandment (2:16-17), transgression and fall (3). The formula 'created after the image' was adjudicated at Mosiah 7:27 and used again at Alma 18:34, and the argument for its preposition is made there; what is new at 22:12 is that the image-clause is now one term of a four-term narrative summary rather than a standalone doctrine, and that the summary's connective term, 'transgression', is Paul's word for the fall and not Genesis's.

22:13.text: But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name:

provenance.other: “believe on his name” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 1:12. The near neighbours differ by a word that matters: 1 John 3:23 has 'believe on the name of his Son Jesus Christ', John 2:23 'believed in his name'. “from the foundation of the world” occurs in six KJV verses and cannot on its own point to one of them; the collocation with 'prepared' is Matthew 25:34's, and that pairing was adjudicated at Alma 12:25 and 13:3.
provenance.significance: The clause that closes Aaron's precis of the plan of redemption is the clause that closes John's prologue, and John 1:12 is about what happens to those outside the covenant people — 'his own received him not, but as many as received him' — which is the situation of a Lamanite king being read the scriptures for the first time. The prologue's next verse is the one the king will quote back at 22:15 when he asks to be 'born of God'.

22:13.note: 'The plan of redemption, which was prepared from the foundation of the world, through Christ, for all whosoever would believe on his name.' Two KJV formulas are joined. The first, 'prepared from the foundation of the world', is Matthew 25:34's and has already been adjudicated in this book at 12:25 and 13:3; it is recorded here as a composite rather than argued again. The second is the finding: 'believe on his name' is John 1:12's alone, and it arrives two verses before the king asks to be 'born of God', which is John 1:13's phrase for the same people. Confidence is moderate because 'believe on his name' is by this point stock Book of Mormon diction and its first adoption is not in Alma; the argument here is for the pairing with the prologue, not for a fresh borrowing.

22:14.text: So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory.

provenance.mt: Isaiah 25:8, 'He will swallow up death in victory'; Hosea 13:14, 'O death, I will be thy plagues; O grave, I will be thy destruction'.
provenance.route: Isaiah 25:8 + Hosea 13:14 → 1 Corinthians 15:54-55 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “swallowed up in victory” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 15:54, and “sting of death” in exactly one, 1 Corinthians 15:56. Isaiah 25:8 has the swallowing and the victory but as an act God performs on death ('He will swallow up death in victory'), not as a state death is put into; Hosea 13:14, which supplies Paul's taunt, has neither 'sting' nor 'victory' in the KJV's Old Testament wording. tools/mediation-check.py returns two decisive points for 1 Corinthians 15:54 and none for Isaiah.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon does not quote Paul's sentences; it redistributes his nouns. Paul's taunt pairs death with sting and grave with victory — 'O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?' — and Alma 22:14 keeps that pairing exactly ('the grave shall have no victory ... the sting of death') while converting both rhetorical questions into flat statements and swapping the object of the swallowing: in Paul death is swallowed up in victory, here the sting of death is swallowed up in the hopes of glory. Recover Paul's context and the substitution reads as a deliberate softening for a catechumen. Paul's 'victory' is eschatological fact addressed to believers who already have the resurrection; 'the hopes of glory' is what a king who has not yet believed can be offered, and it is Colossians 1:27's phrase for Christ in the Gentiles. The chapter is teaching 1 Corinthians 15 to a man being told the plan for the first time, and it lowers the register accordingly.

22:14.note: 'He breaketh the bands of death, that the grave shall have no victory, and that the sting of death should be swallowed up in the hopes of glory.' Four of Paul's terms — grave, victory, sting, death, swallowed up — arrive together in one clause, and three of the phrases built from them are KJV singletons in 1 Corinthians 15. Hardy's apparatus cross-references 1 Corinthians 15:54-55 at this verse. Mediation is the interesting call and it is not close: Paul is quoting Isaiah 25:8 and Hosea 13:14, and every distinctive word the Book of Mormon has here is Paul's rather than the Old Testament's — 'sting' and 'grave' and 'victory' as a trio exist only in 1 Corinthians 15:55-56. Note that no clause is reproduced entire, so this falls well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his long quotations; what makes it certain is the density of singletons, not the length of any run. The 1830 reading 'atoneth' (1920 'atone') is the first edition's, and the '&c.' after 'through faith and repentance' is a compositor's abbreviation the later editions expand to 'and'.

22:15.text: And, behold, one came and said unto him, Good Master, what good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life?

provenance.other: “that I may have eternal life” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 19:16 — Mark 10:17 and Luke 18:18 both read 'inherit' instead. “what shall I do that” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 10:17. So the Book of Mormon's single question carries the interrogative of Mark's version and the verb of Matthew's, and Luke 18:18 supplies what neither of the others does: the questioner is 'a certain ruler'. “great possessions” occurs in three KJV verses, one of them Ecclesiastes 2:7 and the other two Matthew 19:22 and Mark 10:22, both of the same man.
provenance.significance: This is the rich young ruler, asked and answered the other way. In all three gospels a ruler asks what he must do for eternal life, is told to give up what he has, and goes away sorrowful because he had great possessions; here a ruler asks the same question in the same words and volunteers the answer before it is demanded of him — 'I will give up all that I possess; yea, I will forsake my kingdom.' The metalepsis is in what the source withholds. Matthew's man is offered perfection and declines it; Alma's king is offered nothing yet and offers everything, and the thing he offers is precisely the thing the gospel story says a man in his position cannot give. That the Book of Mormon should stage the reversal on a Lamanite rather than a Nephite is the whole burden of Alma 17-26.

22:15.note: 'What shall I do, that I may have this Eternal life of which thou hast spoken? ... I will give up all that I possess; yea, I will forsake my kingdom.' Two KJV singletons meet in one sentence: 'that I may have eternal life' is Matthew 19:16's alone (Mark and Luke read 'inherit'), and 'what shall I do that' is Mark 10:17's alone. The rest of the pericope follows: Luke's questioner is a ruler, and this one is a king; Matthew's and Mark's man has great possessions and will not part with them, and this one offers his kingdom unasked. The second half of the verse ('that I may be born of God') reaches instead for John 1:13, two verses past the phrase Aaron had used at 22:13, which is why John is recorded as a composite here rather than a separate link.

22:16.text: And all things, whatsoever ye shall ask in prayer, believing, ye shall receive.

provenance.other: “believing ye shall receive” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 21:22. Mark 11:24 says the same thing in different words — 'believe that ye receive them, and ye shall have them' — so the Book of Mormon's clause is Matthew's and not the synoptic commonplace.
provenance.significance: Matthew 21:22 is the promise attached to the withered fig tree, given to disciples who have just asked how the tree died so soon: the answer is that faith without doubting moves mountains and that whatsoever you ask believing, you receive. Aaron applies it to a man who has asked for something no mountain-moving is required for, and the condition he attaches — 'bow down before God ... repent of all thy sins ... call on his name in faith' — turns Matthew's promise about petition into a formula for conversion. The 1830's own spelling, 'recieve' twice, is the compositor's; the 1920 addition of 'wilt' before 'bow down' tidies a repetition the first edition left standing.

22:16.note: 'Call on his name in faith, believing that ye shall recieve, then shalt thou recieve the hope which thou desirest.' 'Believing, ye shall receive' is Matthew 21:22's alone in the KJV, and it arrives here as the operative clause of Aaron's instruction. What the Book of Mormon changes is the object: Matthew promises that you will receive the thing asked for, Aaron promises that you will receive 'the hope which thou desirest', which is a hope and not a thing. The machine streams did not propose this verse; the run is short and split by 'that ye shall'.

22:17.text: But let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and cry mightily unto God: yea, let them turn every one from his evil way, and from the violence that is in their hands.

provenance.other: “cry mightily” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jonah 3:8, in the decree of the king of Nineveh. Revelation 18:2's 'cried mightily with a strong voice' is the only other KJV occurrence of the collocation in any inflection, and its speaker is an angel announcing a city's destruction rather than a man praying.
provenance.significance: This is the same KJV singleton that stands behind Alma 9:25, and it is here for the opposite reason. At 9:25 the argument was that the Book of Mormon had redirected Jonah's phrase away from its object — Nineveh cries mightily unto God, Alma's messengers cry mightily unto the people. At 22:17 the phrase goes home. The man crying mightily is a heathen king; he abases himself bodily, as the king of Nineveh rises from his throne and sits in ashes at Jonah 3:6; and ten verses later he 'sent a proclamation throughout all the land, amongst all his people', which is Jonah 3:7's decree proclaimed through Nineveh by the king and his nobles. The whole Ninevite sequence — king humbled, king decrees, city spared — runs through Alma 22-23, and the phrase that was pointed the wrong way at 9:25 is pointed the right way here.

22:17.note: 'The king did bow down before the Lord, upon his knees; yea, even he did prostrate himself upon the earth, and cried mightily.' 'Cry mightily' is Jonah 3:8's alone in the KJV, and the Book of Mormon has already used it once in this book, at 9:25. This is not that formula recurring. ADJUDICATING §4 distinguishes a narrator reusing his own phrase from a phrase returning to its source, and this is the second: 9:25 borrowed the words of a heathen king's decree and gave them to preachers addressing a city, and 22:17 gives them back to a heathen king, on his face, praying — with the proclamation through all his land following at 22:27 as it follows at Jonah 3:7. Judged as a fresh borrowing the verbal contact would be two words; judged as the completion of the Jonah frame Alma 8-9 opened, it is the chapter's structural argument.

22:18.text: Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ,

provenance.other: There is no rare string here; the case is one of sequence. Philippians 3:8-11 runs: the loss of all things — 'that I may know him' — 'if by any means I might attain unto the resurrection of the dead'. Alma 22:18 runs: 'I will give away all my sins to know thee, and that I may be raised from the dead'. 'Raised from the dead' occurs in eight KJV verses and settles nothing on its own; the three steps in that order are what the link rests on.
provenance.significance: The substitution is the finding. Paul gives away all things to know Christ; the king gives away all his sins. Read Paul's context and the swap is pointed — what Paul counts as loss is his pedigree and his righteousness under the law, the assets of a man who had nothing to repent of, and the king has no such inventory to surrender. He is at 22:15 a rich young ruler who offers his kingdom, and at 22:18, three verses later, he has found that the thing actually asked of him is not the kingdom. The line is the most quoted sentence in the chapter and the reason is this compression: the Pauline renunciation with the object changed from possessions to sins.

22:18.note: 'I will give away all my sins to know thee, and that I may be raised from the dead, and be saved at the last day.' Philippians 3:8-11 is the only KJV passage that puts these three in this order — surrender everything, in order to know him, in order to attain the resurrection of the dead — and the king's prayer reproduces the sequence in one sentence. The verbal contact is thin, which is why this is moderate rather than high and why kjvSpecific is 'uncertain': 'know thee' and 'raised from the dead' are common English. What is not common is a prayer that makes knowledge of God the purpose of a renunciation and resurrection the purpose of the knowledge. Compare Hays on metalepsis: the reader who recovers Philippians 3 gets the king's inventory as the one Paul does not have.
22:18.whyNot: No phrase here is distinctive, and the sequence could be assembled from ordinary conversion diction without Philippians in view. A reader could reasonably decline the link and read the verse as the chapter's own composition out of the material of 22:15-16.

22:22.text: But Jesus took him by the hand, and lifted him up; and he arose.

provenance.other: “he was as one dead” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 9:26; “took him by the hand and lifted him up” occurs in exactly one, Mark 9:27. “received strength” occurs in two, Acts 3:7 and Hebrews 11:11, and only Acts 3:7 is a raising. “stand upright on thy feet” occurs in exactly one, Acts 14:10.
provenance.significance: Three KJV raisings are fused, and each contributes the element the others lack. Mark 9:26-27 supplies the frame: a body that onlookers take for a corpse, and a hand that lifts it. Acts 3:7 supplies the strength that returns to the feet. Acts 14:10 supplies the imperative 'Stand' — and Acts 14 is already the chapter this book has been working, since Alma 18:2 was adjudicated against Acts 14:11, where the crowd that sees a man stand upright cries that the gods are come down in the likeness of men. That is precisely the misunderstanding Aaron is racing to prevent at 22:22, and the verse he borrows from is the verse that produces it.

22:22.note: 'He put forth his hand and raised the king from the earth, and said unto him, Stand: and he stood upon his feet, recieving his strength.' The king has lain 'as if he were dead' since 22:18, which is Mark 9:26's situation and its KJV singleton; the raising is Mark 9:27's gesture; the word for what returns to his feet is Acts 3:7's. Alma 15:11 has already used the Acts 3 raising for Zeezrom and Alma 18:42 has already used Mark 9:26 for Lamoni, so the components are not new to the book — what is new is that they are combined, and that the combination is performed under threat, to disperse a mob rather than to heal a man. The 1830 spelling 'recieving' is the compositor's; 1920 corrects it and also deletes the 'and' before 'there should be a great contention'.

22:24.text: And there was much murmuring among the people concerning him: for some said, He is a good man: others said, Nay; but he deceiveth the people.

provenance.other: “there was much murmuring” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 7:12, and it is the KJV's only instance of murmuring as the sound of a crowd divided over a teacher rather than of Israel complaining against Moses. The Book of Mormon's 'there began to be great murmurings among them' substitutes 'great' for 'much' and pluralizes the noun, which is why this is an echo and not an allusion.
provenance.significance: John 7 is the chapter where a crowd assembles about a teacher whose fate is undecided, splits over whether he is a good man or a deceiver, and is restrained because nobody dares lay hands on him. Alma 22:20-26 has the same three beats in the same order — the servants who 'durst not lay their hands on Aaron', the multitude gathered and murmuring, the crowd pacified — which is more than the shared phrase would carry on its own and is the reason the echo is worth recording.

22:24.note: 'There began to be great murmurings among them, because of Aaron and his brethren.' The KJV reserves 'murmuring' almost entirely for Israel in the wilderness; John 7:12 is the exception, and it is the exception that fits — a crowd gathered about preachers, divided about them, and not yet violent. The verbal contact is one substituted adjective away from exact and the link is recorded as an echo on that account. What raises it above the wording is the surrounding shape: at 22:20 the servants 'durst not lay their hands' on the brethren, which is John 7:30's and 7:44's refrain about the same crowd.
